references.text: God saw that the wickedness of man was great on the earth, and that every thought and plan in their hearts was evil all day long.
The earth was corrupt before God; the earth was filled with violence.
Then God said to Noah, 'I have decided to put an end to all people, for the earth is full of violence because of them. Look, I will destroy them along with the earth.'
The Lord looks down from heaven on humanity to find someone who is wise, one who seeks God. They have all turned away; all are corrupt. No one does good, not even one.
He said to me, 'Do you see this, son of man? Is it not enough for the house of Judah to do the detestable things they have done here, that they also fill the land with violence?'

By faith Noah, being warned by God about events not yet seen, in reverent fear built an ark to save his household. By this faith he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes from faith.
Thematic connection between the corruption of the earth as the cause and the destruction of the earth as the result of judgment.
Contrast between the original goodness of creation and the subsequent total corruption.
Contrast between the goodness of creation and the corruption that affects all flesh.
Theological parallel about human sin destroying the earth and triggering God's judgment.
Connection between the basis for judgment (corruption) and the just nature of the judgment itself.
Contrast between a world where everyone is corrupt (Gen 6) and a world where the righteous still suffer (Ecc).
Theological contrast between collective judgment (the flood) and individual responsibility (Ezekiel).
Strong parallel that the condition of the earth reflects human sin and triggers God's punishment.
Theological connection between the entry of sin (Rom) and its global consequence (Gen 6).
A strong parallel that the destruction of the earth is a direct consequence of human guilt.
Theological connection between the question of God's righteous wrath (Rom) and its basis (Gen 6).
Connection between the basis for judgment (corruption) and the just nature of the judgment itself.
Direct allusion to 'judgment on all flesh' referring to the situation in Genesis 6.
Connection between the basis for judgment (corruption) and the nature of the judgment itself (to punish the ungodly).
Theological contrast between corrupt flesh that triggers judgment (Gen 6) and God's Son in flesh who resolves sin (Rom).
